summary: This program models a browser's history with an ArrayDeque of URLs, adding pages to the front as they are visited, then removing the current page from the front (going back) and discarding the two oldest pages from the back. It shows that a Deque lets you add and remove at either end.

lines.text: Java keywords are case-sensitive, so this must be written as `import` with a lowercase i; as printed, the compiler rejects the file. The runnable copy of this exercise fixes the capital letter.
The variable is declared with the Deque interface but built with the ArrayDeque implementation, so the code depends only on the double-ended queue behaviour and not on the class behind it.
addFirst pushes a URL onto the front of the deque, which is how a browser records the page you just visited.
Because every page was added at the front, the blog page is now the newest entry and home is the oldest.
forEach walks the deque from front to back, so the pages print newest first; System.out::println is a method reference standing in for a one-line lambda.
pollFirst removes and returns the front element, simulating the Back button leaving the current page. It returns null instead of throwing if the deque is empty.

lines.code: System.out.println("\nGo back: remove current page (front): " + lastVisited);
lines.text: The \n escape prints a blank line before the text, which keeps the three sections of output visually separate.
pollLast removes from the opposite end, so this trims the oldest visited page — the kind of housekeeping a browser does when its history grows too long.
